subtitle: Midterm Important Subjective Questions (Solved)
topics: Introduction and the Role of Simulation

subjective.topic: Introduction and the Role of Simulation
subjective.question: What is a model? Why do we study a system through a model instead of experimenting with the real system itself?
subjective.answer: A model is a representation of a system for the purpose of studying the system. For most studies it is only necessary to consider those aspects of the system that affect the problem under investigation, so a model is by definition a simplification of the system — yet it must be sufficiently detailed to permit valid conclusions to be drawn about the real system. Experimenting with the real system is often impossible or impractical: the system may not yet exist (it may be only in hypothetical or design form, e.g. a space flight system); it may be too costly (e.g. investing $200 million in a loading/unloading berth just to test whether it is adequate); or it may be disruptive or unacceptable (e.g. doubling the unemployment rate to study inflation, or reducing the number of tellers in a bank and infuriating customers). A model avoids all of these problems.

subjective.topic: Introduction and the Role of Simulation
subjective.question: When is simulation an appropriate tool? Give the main reasons for using simulation.
subjective.answer: Simulation is an appropriate tool in many situations: (1) it enables the study of, and experimentation with, the internal interactions of a complex system, or of a subsystem within a complex system — modern systems such as factories, wafer fabrication plants and service organizations are so complex that their internal interactions can be treated only through simulation; (2) informational, organizational and environmental changes can be simulated and their effect on the model's behaviour observed; (3) the knowledge gained in designing a simulation model can suggest improvements in the real system; (4) changing inputs and observing outputs gives insight into which variables are most important and how variables interact; (5) it can be used as a pedagogical device to reinforce analytic solution methodologies, and to verify analytic solutions; (6) it allows experimentation with new designs or policies before implementation; (7) simulating different capabilities of a machine helps determine the requirements on it; (8) models designed for training make learning possible without the cost and disruption of on-the-job instruction; and (9) animation shows the system in simulated operation so that a plan can be visualized.

subjective.topic: Introduction and the Role of Simulation
subjective.question: State the ten rules of Banks and Gibson (1997) for when simulation is NOT appropriate.
subjective.answer: (1) Simulation should not be used when the problem can be solved by common sense. (2) It should not be used if the problem can be solved analytically. (3) It should not be used if it is easier to perform direct experiments. (4) It should not be used if the costs exceed the savings. (5) and (6) It should not be performed if the resources or the time are not available. (7) It should not be used if no data is available, not even estimates — simulation takes data, sometimes lots of data. (8) It should not be used if there is not enough time or personnel to verify and validate the model. (9) It should not be used if managers have unreasonable expectations, ask for too much too soon, or overestimate the power of simulation. (10) It should not be used if system behaviour is too complex or cannot be defined. In short, simulation should be used only when it is the most appropriate tool for the problem.

subjective.topic: Introduction and the Role of Simulation
subjective.question: List the main advantages of simulation (as summarized by Pegden, Shannon and Sadowski).
subjective.answer: (1) New policies, operating procedures, decision rules, information flows and organizational procedures can be explored without disrupting ongoing operations of the real system. (2) New hardware designs, physical layouts and transportation systems can be tested without committing resources for their acquisition. (3) Hypotheses about how or why certain phenomena occur can be tested for feasibility. (4) Time can be compressed or expanded, allowing a speed-up or slow-down of the phenomena under investigation. (5) Insight can be obtained about the interaction of variables. (6) Insight can be obtained about the importance of variables to the performance of the system. (7) Bottleneck analysis can be performed to discover where work in process, information and materials are being delayed excessively. (8) A simulation study can help in understanding how the system actually operates, rather than how individuals think it operates. (9) "What if" questions can be answered, which is particularly useful in the design of new systems.

subjective.topic: Introduction and the Role of Simulation
subjective.question: What are the main disadvantages of simulation? How can they be defended against?
subjective.answer: The disadvantages are: (1) Model building requires special training — it is an art learned over time and through experience, and two models built by different competent individuals are highly unlikely to be identical. (2) Simulation results can be difficult to interpret, because most simulation outputs are essentially random variables based on random inputs, so it can be hard to tell whether an observation results from system interrelationships or from randomness. (3) Simulation modeling and analysis can be time consuming and expensive, and skimping on resources can produce a model or analysis that is not sufficient for the task. (4) Simulation is sometimes used when an analytical solution is possible or even preferable, e.g. for some waiting lines where closed-form queueing models are available. In defense: vendors have developed packages containing generic "simulator" or "template" models that need only input data, with thorough built-in output-analysis capabilities; simulation runs faster every year because of advances in hardware and software; and closed-form models are not able to analyze most of the complex systems encountered in practice.

subjective.question: Define a system and explain the following components of a system: entity, attribute, activity, state and event. Also distinguish between endogenous and exogenous activities and events.
subjective.answer: A system is a group of objects joined together in some regular interaction or interdependence toward the accomplishment of some purpose. An entity is any object of interest in the system (e.g. a server, a customer or a machine). An attribute is the property of an entity (e.g. the priority of a waiting customer). An activity represents a time period of a specific length (e.g. a service time). The state of a system is the collection of variables necessary to describe the system at any time, relative to the objectives of the study. An event is an instantaneous occurrence that might change the state of the system (e.g. the arrival of a customer). The terms endogenous and exogenous distinguish where things happen: endogenous refers to activities and events occurring within the system, while exogenous refers to activities and events occurring in the environment that affect the system.

subjective.question: Distinguish between discrete and continuous systems, giving one example of each.
subjective.answer: A discrete system is one in which the state variables change only at a discrete set of points in time. Example: in a bank, the state variable "number of customers" changes only when a customer arrives or when a service is completed. A continuous system is one in which the state variables change continuously over time. Example: the head of water behind a dam changes continuously as rain flows in or the dam is emptied. In practice, few systems are wholly discrete or wholly continuous, but since one type of change predominates for most systems, a system can usually be classified as one or the other (Law and Kelton).

subjective.question: How are simulation models classified? Explain static vs dynamic, deterministic vs stochastic, and discrete vs continuous models.
subjective.answer: A simulation model is a special type of mathematical model, and simulation models are classified as static or dynamic, deterministic or stochastic, and discrete or continuous. A static simulation model, sometimes called a Monte Carlo simulation, represents a system at a particular point in time, whereas a dynamic simulation model represents a system as it changes over time (e.g. simulating a bank from 9 AM to 2 PM). A deterministic model contains no random variables: it has a known set of inputs which results in a unique set of outputs (e.g. patients arriving exactly at their scheduled appointment times at a dentist's office). A stochastic model has one or more random variables as inputs; random inputs lead to random outputs, so the outputs must be treated as statistical estimates of the true characteristics of the system (e.g. a bank with random interarrival and service times). Discrete and continuous models are defined analogously to discrete and continuous systems, although a discrete model is not always used for a discrete system and vice versa — the choice depends on the characteristics of the system and the objective of the study. This course primarily studies discrete, dynamic and stochastic models.

subjective.question: List the steps in a simulation study in order.
subjective.answer: The steps in a simulation study are: (1) Problem formulation; (2) Setting of objectives and overall project plan; (3) Model conceptualization; (4) Data collection; (5) Model translation; (6) Verification; (7) Validation; (8) Experimental design; (9) Production runs and analysis; (10) More runs? (deciding whether additional runs are needed); (11) Documentation and reporting; (12) Implementation.

subjective.question: What guidelines should be followed in model conceptualization?
subjective.answer: Building a model is as much art as science, but some general guidelines (Morris, 1967) can be followed. The art of modeling is enhanced by an ability to abstract the essential features of a problem, to select and modify the basic assumptions that characterize the system, and to enrich and elaborate the model until a useful approximation results. It is best to start with a simple model and build toward greater complexity; however, model complexity should not exceed what is required for the purposes of the study, since violating this principle only adds to model-building and computer expense. There is no need for a one-to-one mapping between the model and the real system — only the essence of the real system is needed. Finally, the model user should be involved in model conceptualization: this enhances the quality of the resulting model and increases the user's confidence in its application.

subjective.question: Distinguish between verification and validation in a simulation study.
subjective.answer: Verification pertains to the computer program prepared for the simulation model: the basic question is "Is the computer program performing properly?" With complex models it is difficult to translate a model successfully in its entirety without a good deal of debugging; if the input parameters and the logical structure of the model are correctly represented in the computer, verification has been completed. Validation, on the other hand, is concerned with whether the model represents the real system accurately. It is usually achieved through calibration — an iterative process of comparing the model against actual system behaviour and using the discrepancies between the two, and the insights gained, to improve the model. This process is repeated until model accuracy is judged acceptable. For example, in a bank study, data on the length of waiting lines under current conditions can be compared with the waiting lines produced by the model.

subjective.question: What decisions are made in the experimental design step of a simulation study? What is the purpose of production runs and analysis?
subjective.answer: In experimental design, the alternatives (system designs) that are to be simulated must first be determined — often as a function of runs already completed and analyzed. For each system design that is simulated, decisions need to be made concerning the length of the initialization period, the length of the simulation runs, and the number of replications to be made for each run. Production runs, and their subsequent analysis, are then used to estimate measures of performance for the system designs that are being simulated. After analyzing the completed runs, the analyst determines whether additional runs are needed and what design those additional experiments should follow.

subjective.question: What is discrete-event simulation? How does it differ from analytical solution of a model?
subjective.answer: Discrete-event system simulation is the modeling of systems in which the state variable changes only at a discrete set of points in time. The system is modeled in terms of its state at each point in time, the entities that pass through the system and represent its resources, and the activities and events that cause the system state to change. Such models are analyzed by numerical methods rather than analytical methods. Analytical methods employ the deductive reasoning of mathematics to "solve" the model (e.g. using differential calculus to compute a minimum-cost inventory policy), whereas numerical methods employ computational procedures: the simulation model is "run" rather than solved, an artificial history of the system is generated from the model assumptions, and observations are collected, analyzed and used to estimate the true system performance measures. Because real-world models are large and manipulate vast amounts of data, the runs are usually conducted with the aid of a computer, although much insight can be obtained by simulating small models manually.

subjective.question: Define the following discrete-event simulation concepts: event notice, event list (FEL), activity, delay and CLOCK.
subjective.answer: An event notice is a record of an event to occur at the current or some future time, together with any associated data necessary to execute the event; at a minimum, the record includes the event type and the event time. An event list is a list of event notices for future events, ordered by time of occurrence; it is also known as the future event list (FEL). An activity is a duration of time of specified length (e.g. a service time or an interarrival time) which is known when it begins, although it may be defined in terms of a statistical distribution. A delay is a duration of time of unspecified indefinite length, which is not known until it ends (e.g. a customer's delay in a waiting line); a delay is sometimes called a conditional wait, while an activity is an unconditional wait. CLOCK is the variable representing simulated time. The FEL is always ranked by the event time recorded in the event notice, while lists of entities are ordered by some rule such as first-in-first-out, last-in-first-out, or priority.

subjective.question: Explain the event-scheduling / time-advance algorithm.
subjective.answer: The mechanism for advancing simulation time and guaranteeing that all events occur in correct chronological order is based on the future event list (FEL), which contains all event notices for events scheduled to occur at a future time, ordered by event time. Let t be the current value of CLOCK and t1 the smallest event time on the FEL; the event associated with t1 is called the imminent event. The algorithm proceeds as follows: (1) remove the imminent event notice from the FEL; (2) advance CLOCK to t1; (3) execute the imminent event, creating a new system snapshot for time t1 based on the old snapshot and the nature of the event — this updates the system state, entity attributes and set contents; (4) generate any new future events, scheduling them by creating event notices and inserting them into their proper position on the FEL. This process repeats — advance to the new imminent event, execute it, update the snapshot — until the simulation is over. When using the event-scheduling approach, the analyst concentrates on events and their effect on system state.

subjective.question: What is bootstrapping? Distinguish between primary and conditional events, and explain the two ways of defining the stopping event E.
subjective.answer: Bootstrapping is the method of generating an external arrival stream in a simulation: at time 0 the first arrival event is generated and placed on the FEL; when the clock advances to that arrival, a new interarrival time a* is generated, and the next arrival event is scheduled at t* = t + a*. The end of an interarrival interval (and likewise a service completion) is a primary event — the completion of an activity, managed by placing an event notice on the FEL. A conditional (secondary) event, such as the beginning of service, is triggered only when certain conditions hold (a customer is present and a server is free); the completion of a delay is a conditional event and is not represented by an event notice on the FEL. Every simulation must have a stopping event E, defined in one of two ways: either a "stop simulation" event is scheduled at time 0 for a specified future time TE (e.g. simulate a job shop for 40 hours), or the run length is determined by the simulation itself, TE being the time of occurrence of some specified event (e.g. the 100th service completion at a service centre, or the breakdown of a complex system).

subjective.question: Name the three world views used in developing simulation models, and explain the three-phase approach.
subjective.answer: The most prevalent world views are the event-scheduling world view, the process-interaction world view and the activity-scanning world view. In the process-interaction view, the analyst thinks in terms of processes — a process is the life cycle of one entity, a time-sequenced list of events, activities and delays (including demands for resources) as the entity flows through the system. The activity-scanning approach has been modified into the three-phase approach, which combines features of event scheduling with activity scanning. In the three-phase approach, events are considered activities of duration zero, and activities are divided into B activities (bound to occur: all primary events and unconditional activities, which can be scheduled ahead of time on the FEL) and C activities (conditional upon certain conditions being true). The simulation proceeds by repeated execution of three phases: Phase A — remove the imminent event (and any others with the same event time) from the FEL and advance the clock to its event time; Phase B — execute all B-type events that were removed (this may free resources or otherwise change the system state); Phase C — scan the conditions that trigger each C-type activity and activate any whose conditions are met, rescanning until no additional C-type activities can begin. These approaches are claimed to be particularly good at handling complex resource problems, guaranteeing that all resources freed at a given simulated time are freed before any are reallocated.

subjective.question: Describe the manual simulation of the single-channel (checkout counter) queue using event scheduling. How is server utilization computed, and what were the results over the interval [0, 23]?
subjective.answer: In manual simulation using event scheduling, a simulation table is used to record the successive system snapshots as time advances. For the grocery store with one checkout counter, the system consists of the customers in the waiting line plus the one (if any) checking out; the event notices are written as (event type, event time), and the FEL always contains two or three notices (the next arrival, the next departure, and the stop event at time 60). Two statistics are collected: server utilization and maximum queue length. Server utilization is defined as the total server busy time B divided by the total time TE. Initially the first customer arrives at time 0 and begins service, so LQ(0) = 0 and LS(0) = 1. Executing the arrival and departure events step by step over the interval [0, 23], the server was busy for 21 of the 23 time units, giving a utilization of 21/23, and the maximum queue length was two. At time 23 the system empties just as the next arrival occurs. Such a short simulation is, of course, too short to draw reliable conclusions.

subjective.question: Define a discrete random variable and its probability mass function (pmf). Illustrate with the loaded-die example.
subjective.answer: Let X be a random variable. If the number of possible values of X is finite, or countably infinite, X is called a discrete random variable; its possible values x1, x2, ... form its range space RX. With each possible outcome xi, a number p(xi) = P(X = xi) gives the probability that the random variable equals xi. The collection of pairs (xi, p(xi)) is called the probability distribution of X, and p(xi) is called the probability mass function (pmf) of X. The pmf must satisfy two conditions: p(xi) ≥ 0 for all i, and the sum of all p(xi) equals 1. Example: toss a single die and let X be the number of spots on the up face, so RX = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}. If the die is loaded so that the probability of a face is proportional to the number of spots showing, then p(xi) = i/21, i.e. 1/21, 2/21, ..., 6/21, which indeed sums to 21/21 = 1.

subjective.question: Define expectation, variance, standard deviation and mode of a random variable.
subjective.answer: The expectation (expected value) E(X) of a random variable is its mean, denoted μ, and is also called the first moment of X; the expectation of X^n is the nth moment. The mean is a measure of the central tendency of the random variable. The variance V(X) measures the spread or variation of the possible values of X around the mean: it is the expected value of the squared difference between the random variable and its mean. The standard deviation σ is defined as the square root of the variance, σ = √V(X); the mean and the standard deviation have the same units. The mode is used in describing several statistical models: in the discrete case, the mode is the value of the random variable that occurs most frequently; in the continuous case, it is the value at which the pdf is maximized. The mode might not be unique — if the modal value occurs at two values, the distribution is said to be bimodal.

subjective.question: What properties should random numbers used in simulation have? What is a random number generator?
subjective.answer: Because almost every simulation needs at least one random variable, randomness must be generated carefully. In the real world, the number of factors involved in any event is so numerous that such events are very difficult to predict, and in a computer true randomness is very hard to generate — hence the concept of pseudo-randomness. A random number is a generated number between 0 and 1, and a random variable is any randomly generated quantity with a specified statistical distribution. A method of generating a sequence of random numbers is called a Random Number Generator (RNG). Two important statistical properties are required: the numbers should be uniformly distributed between 0 and 1, and subsequent numbers should be statistically independent of all previous numbers. In spreadsheet simulation, functions such as RAND() in Excel are used for this purpose; for manual simulation, a coin toss or dice can be used, though these are impractical for anything large.

subjective.question: What is agent-based modeling (ABM)? Define an agent and explain the role of the environment and interactions.
subjective.answer: Agent-based modeling is a form of computational modeling whereby a phenomenon is modeled in terms of agents and their interactions. An agent is an autonomous computational individual or object with particular properties and actions — more precisely, an autonomous individual element of a computer simulation that has properties (state variables with values), states, and rules of behaviour. For example, a gas molecule agent might have properties mass, speed and heading, and a rule to collide with other molecules; a sheep agent might have speed, weight and fleece, and a rule to eat grass if grass is available nearby. The environment is the landscape on which agents interact; it can be geometric, network-based, or drawn from real data. Agents interact with other agents and with the environment, and both their interaction behaviours and the strategies used to decide actions can change over time. In an agent-based model there is a universal clock: when the clock ticks, all agents invoke their rules, and if the conditions of a rule are satisfied, the agent enacts the behaviour.

subjective.question: What is emergence? Discuss its important features and the two challenges in understanding emergent phenomena.
subjective.answer: Through the interaction of multiple distributed elements, an "emergent phenomenon" arises. Emergence is defined as the arising of novel and coherent structures, patterns and properties through the interactions of multiple distributed elements (the term "emergent" was coined by the British philosopher and psychologist G. H. Lewes). Important features of emergence include: the global pattern's spontaneous arising from the interaction of the elements, and the absence of an orchestrator or centralized coordinator — the system self-organizes. Structure (rules) at the micro-level leads to ordered pattern at the macro-level, and because the macrostructures are composed of many elements they are dynamic, often reforming when perturbed. Emergence presents two fundamental and distinct challenges: integrative understanding — figuring out the aggregate pattern when one knows how the individual elements behave; and differential (compositional) understanding — when the aggregate pattern is known, finding the behaviour of the elements that could generate it. People's difficulty with these challenges is linked to the deterministic-centralized (DC) mindset and to "thinking in levels" — slipping between the level of individual elements and the level of aggregate patterns.

subjective.question: Compare agent-based models with equation-based models. What is the "nano-wolf" problem?
subjective.answer: The most common form of scientific model is the equation (equational) form, e.g. the Lotka–Volterra differential equations for predator–prey dynamics. Agent-based models differ in several ways. First, because an ABM models individuals, it can model a heterogeneous population, whereas equational models typically must make assumptions of homogeneity. Second, when individuals are modeled, interactions and results are typically discrete rather than continuous, and continuous models do not always map well onto real-world situations: equation-based models of population dynamics treat populations as continuous quantities, although real populations consist of discrete individuals. This causes the "nano-wolf" problem (Wilson, 1998): a wolf population cannot continue if fewer than two wolves remain, yet in an equation-based model a millionth of a wolf can exist and even reproduce, so the equational model under-represents extinctions. ABMs also make their mechanisms explicit and do not require calculus, making them accessible entry points into scientific domains. On the other hand, for an expert an equation can represent a phenomenon more compactly, and when solvable it enables direct calculation of results without running a model; ABMs can also be computationally intensive, since simulating thousands or millions of individuals requires great computing power. As a rule of thumb, agent-based models are most useful when there are a medium number (tens to millions) of interacting agents.

subjective.question: Describe Conway's Game of Life: its setup and rules. What is a "glider"?
subjective.answer: The Game of Life, devised by the British mathematician John Horton Conway in 1970 and popularized by Martin Gardner, is a cellular automaton — an interesting first (toy) agent-based model. It is played on a large grid (e.g. 51 × 51 cells). Each cell can be either "alive" or "dead" — this is the state of the cell — and every cell is surrounded by eight neighbour cells (the grid wraps around at the edges). There is a central clock; in Life the unit of time is called a generation (in agent-based models generally, a tick). Whenever the clock ticks, each cell updates its state in parallel according to the rules: (1) if a cell has fewer than two alive neighbours, it dies; (2) if it has more than three alive neighbours, it also dies; (3) if it has exactly two alive neighbours, the cell remains in the state it is in; (4) if it has exactly three alive neighbours, the cell becomes alive if it is dead, or stays alive if it is already alive. In NetLogo the model is implemented with patches. Although the rules are extremely simple, complex emergent patterns arise — for example the "glider", a small configuration that moves across the grid.

subjective.question: Explain the Ants (foraging) model: the rules an ant follows, and the emergent behaviour of the colony.
subjective.answer: In the Ants model, each ant follows simple individual rules: (1) if I am not carrying food, I check whether there is food where I am — if there is, I pick it up; if there is not, I try to sense a pheromone trail nearby, and if I find one I face "uphill" along the pheromone gradient toward its strongest source; (2) if I am carrying food, I turn back toward the nest and drop pheromone on the ground below me; (3) I turn randomly a small amount and move forward a step. Initially the ants wander at random; once some ants find a food source they bring food back, laying a pheromone trail. A lone ant's trail is too weak to follow, but as more ants find the source the trail becomes stronger and stronger. The colony as a whole appears to exploit food sources in an optimal manner — gathering first from the nearest source, then the second nearest, and so on — and it balances exploration (some ants keep searching) and exploitation (many ants harvest the known source). These "trails", "optimality" and "balance" behaviours are not coded into any individual ant; they are an emergent phenomenon of the model, arising without any centralized leader — disproving the hypothesis that a queen ant directs the foraging.

subjective.question: Describe the Simple Economy model and its surprising result. What creates the stationary distribution, and how does this connect with econophysics?
subjective.answer: In the Simple Economy model there is a fixed number of people — say 500 — each starting with the same amount of money, say $100. At every tick, each person gives one dollar to any other person chosen at random; no one can have less than zero money, and the total amount of money remains fixed. Intuition suggests a flat limiting distribution (nobody has an advantage, so everyone should end with roughly what they started with) or a normal distribution. In fact, after long runs the distribution is not flat at all: there are a few very wealthy individuals and many poor agents (in one run, the top 10 percent held $12,633 in total while the entire bottom 50 percent held only $10,166), and the distribution converges to a stationary exponential distribution, meaning great inequality in monetary wealth. The key condition creating this stationary distribution is the conservation of money. The model is an instance of a broader class in which a conserved quantity is exchanged in a closed system — the same mathematics Boltzmann developed for gas molecules ("billiard balls") whose energies form the stationary exponential Boltzmann (Boltzmann–Gibbs / Maxwell–Boltzmann) distribution, a central component of statistical mechanics. Applying such physics theories and methods to economics is called econophysics, a term coined by the physicist Gene Stanley (1996). (Empirically, real wealth distributions follow an even more unequal power law — the Pareto distribution — associated with preferential attachment processes.)

subjective.question: Explain the Fire model and the concept of a tipping point.
subjective.answer: The (forest) Fire model arose from efforts to understand percolation phenomena — the movement of a substance (such as oil) through another material (such as rock) with some porosity. The model represents the environment as a grid of cells with trees occupying certain cells, and fire spreads by simple rules from burning cells to neighbouring tree cells. The model is highly sensitive to one parameter: whether or not the fire will burn from one side of the forest to the other (percolate) is mainly dependent on the percentage of the ground covered by trees (the density). As this parameter increases there is little to no effect for a long time, and then suddenly the fire leaps across the world — this is a tipping point: a point at which a small change in one parameter results in a large change in an outcome. Knowing that a system exhibits a tipping point, and how close the system is to it, tells us whether continued effort is likely to bear fruit and whether a small effort can produce a big change. Tipping points are defined relative to a chosen input and output measure — a model does not have a tipping point in and of itself. Extensions of the model add probabilistic spread (a PROBABILITY-OF-SPREAD parameter; setting it to 100 percent reproduces the original model), wind (which raises the spread probability in the direction it blows and lowers it in the opposite direction), and long-distance "big jumps".

subjective.question: Describe Schelling's segregation model and its main lesson.
subjective.answer: Thomas Schelling explored segregation with his Neighborhood Tipping model (1971), using a checkerboard as a grid, pennies to represent one race and dimes to represent another. He assumed that everyone wanted to live where at least a reasonable fraction of their neighbours were like themselves — an aversion to being an extreme minority ("weakly prejudiced"). For each coin he counted the fraction of surrounding neighbours of the same type; if this value fell below a certain threshold, he moved the coin to a random empty location, repeating the process hundreds of times. What surprised Schelling was that even at low threshold levels — despite the relative tolerance of each individual — the pennies and dimes still ended up in dense, segregated clusters. No single individual wanted a segregated neighbourhood, yet the group as a whole moved toward segregation: global segregation is an emergent effect of the aggregation of people's weak prejudice — "macrobehavior" derived from "micromotives" (1978). The model's lesson is that segregation need not be caused by strongly prejudiced individuals; it can emerge from mild individual preferences, so prejudice itself is not necessarily a "leverage point" of the housing system. Schelling was awarded the Nobel Prize in Economics in 2005.
